query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The onset and progression of premelting and melting in initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by surface-driven processes—specifically, selective atomic segregation and surface diffusion. Inhibiting these surface processes (e.g., by capping the nanoparticle surfaces with a passivating agent) will delay the appearance of pre-melting phenomena and shift the melting onset to higher temperatures compared to untreated, bare nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, well-mixed, and homogeneous FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with a narrow size distribution.
generation.intervention: Surface modification using a capping agent that suppresses surface atomic diffusion and segregation, compared to unmodified (bare) nanoparticles.
generation.conditions: Controlled heating in an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) with a well-defined heating rate and constant nanoparticle size distribution; experiments conducted under conditions mimicking the premelting and melting regime of high-temperature synthesis.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface structure and chemistry, particularly the degree of atomic mobility and the potential for selective segregation on nanoparticle surfaces.
generation.mechanism: In bare nanoparticles, surface atoms possess higher mobility at elevated temperatures, promoting early surface diffusion and selective atomic segregation that lead to a premature initiation of phase transition. In contrast, passivated nanoparticles experience hindered surface diffusion, thereby delaying or modifying the progression of the premelting phase and subsequent bulk melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical heating conditions, passivated nanoparticles will exhibit a measurable delay in the onset of pre-melting (evidenced by fewer surface diffusion events and less incipient segregation) and a higher observed melting initiation temperature compared to untreated nanoparticles, which will show earlier surface restructuring and a lower melting onset temperature.
generation.baseline: Baseline behavior is defined by the thermal response of untreated FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles, which are expected to exhibit surface pre-melting phenomena such as atomic diffusion and selective segregation prior to bulk melting.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under controlled high-temperature conditions with rapid and uniform heating rates (typical of high-temperature synthesis), inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation, and nanoparticles with minimal size variation.
generation.uncertainty: There is residual uncertainty regarding the relative contributions of bulk diffusion versus surface processes in the complete melting process; while the hypothesis focuses on surface-driven mechanisms, the interplay with any emerging bulk effects at higher temperatures is not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with identical size distributions: one set having bare surfaces and the other capped with a surface-passivating agent designed to limit atomic diffusion. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature ramp experiments under an inert atmosphere while monitoring the nanoparticles in situ (e.g., using TEM combined with spectroscopic analysis).
measurements: In situ TEM imaging of surface diffusion events and atomic segregation as temperature increases.
Determination of the onset temperature of observable pre-melting phenomena and bulk melting using thermal analysis (e.g., differential scanning calorimetry).
Compositional mapping via energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy to detect segregation changes.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the passivated and bare nanoparticle samples display indistinguishable onset temperatures for pre-melting phenomena, similar extents of surface diffusion and segregation, and nearly identical melting progression profiles under identical experimental conditions, then the hypothesis that surface-driven processes dominate the phase transition onset would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In order to rule out the effect of electromigration on the formation of nanoparticles, rapid radiative heating process was used to synthesize nanoparticles on carbon support. The rapid radiative heating setup is schematically shown in Fig. S5a. In this configuration, the outside carbon film acts as a source for flash high temperature radiation to heat up the S-CNF. At this condition, the salt-loaded CNFs were only exposed to high temperatures under ultrafast heating rate (>105 K/s), and no direct electrical current was applied to the S-CNFs. After rapid radiative heating treatment, the prepared Pt NPs@CNF specimens were analyzed via HRSTEM. As we can see from Fig. S5b, a uniform distribution of small nanoparticles was observed on the CNF support. Similar to the Joule heating case, the amorphous carbon film showed evidence of crystallization and the NPs were associated with the T-graphite edge planes. To summarize, we included the above experiments in Table S1. Overall, it is evident that the formation and stabilization of nanoparticles are governed by the rapid heating process, and not necessarily electromigration. Our work provides direct visualization of nanoparticles on amorphous carbon supports and elucidate the details of amorphous carbon graphitization during ultrafast exposure to extremely high temperatures under electrical Joule heating process. The in situ TEM studies of Joule heating on amorphous carbon fibers loaded with metal precursors show that during the Joule heating process, the CNFs undergo volumetric expansion due to amorphous to crystalline phase transition, which is also associated with formation and stabilization of metallic nanoparticles on the carbon supports. The crystallized CNFs are made of T-graphite with a high density of randomly dispersed edge planes. These edge planes are highly defective and act as preferred sites for the nucleation of metallic nanoparticles. In addition, metal atoms diffuse into layered structure strengthening the anchoring of the nanoparticles on the edge planes. This prevents the nanoparticles from further aggregation at extremely high temperatures as confirmed by MD simulation and in situ heating in TEM. decision.trend: Early HEA nanoparticle studies—especially those aimed at catalytic performance and stabilization under high‐temperature processing—have revealed that surface phenomena are critical to understanding thermal behavior. For example, work reporting on CoMoFeNiCu catalysts (PMC6728353) and in situ nanoparticle formation (PMC7733500) both noted that surface restructuring (including atomic diffusion and selective segregation) can preempt bulk phase transformations. These studies typically employed high-temperature synthesis with rapid heating or Joule heating, finding hints of pre‐melting phenomena (such as the emergence of surface diffusion events and incipient segregation), but were not designed to definitively attribute melting onset solely to surface effects. The historical sequence moved from bulk property characterization to in situ observations indicating the potential role of surface pre‐melting, yet no study so far has tightly controlled or compared surface chemistry effects.
decision.unsolved: It remains unsolved which specific surface-driven mechanisms — particularly the role of selective atomic segregation and surface diffusion — govern the onset and progression of phase transition (premelting to melting) in these complex FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles. In other words, it is unclear how surface chemistry (and by extension, surface energy differences among constituent elements) influences the melting onset under controlled heating and defined nanoparticle size distributions.
decision.lever: Systematically vary and control the nanoparticle surface chemistry (for example, comparing bare nanoparticles versus those coated with a capping agent that inhibits surface atomic diffusion) while maintaining a narrow size distribution and constant heating rate under an inert atmosphere
decision.why: Because prior work has pointed to surface pre-melting and segregation as key precursors to bulk melting, a controlled experiment isolating surface chemistry effects directly addresses the gap. By comparing nanoparticles with intentionally modified surfaces against untreated controls, one can observe shifts in melting onset temperature and pre-melting activity (e.g., detectable via in situ TEM and compositional analyses). The presence of a delayed or altered melting signature in the surface‐passivated sample would support the hypothesis, whereas its absence (i.e., if both samples exhibit identical pre-melting behavior) would falsify it.
